title: Meeting Challenges in Food Production

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By 2050, there will be approximately nine billion people in the world and an essential question is whether we have sufficient land and water to feed them. Unless there are major breakthroughs in terms of crop yields, there will have to be a greater area of land made available for cultivation in order to meet such a rise in demand. Agriculture and livestock are by far the largest water users in the world. It is likely that we will have water shortages in a lot of locations, and farmers are going to have to adopt new technologies and crops to become more conservative in their water use.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: I believe that feedback in the system will bring answers to the food problem. As we start hitting periods of shortages, there is typically more commitment to investment in agriculture to increase productivity. Agricultural markets are dynamic, prices reflect scarcity, and the kind of food we produce and eat can alter. As water becomes scarcer, farmers are probably going to switch to crops that are less water-intensive or that rely on drip irrigation. Or as food prices rise, maybe people won't eat quite as much meat—especially not as much as they eat in the USA—and that will have an impact on the demand side. We can either adapt and start using land and water more efficiently, or people will continue to suffer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There's a big gap between farmers' yields and experimental yields, that is the highest that can be achieved. In places like Nebraska in the USA, farmers are probably close to the yield ceiling on certain crops. But for most of the world — Africa, Asia and Latin America—other constraints are keeping farmers from reaching more than 50 percent of the yields achieved in the USA. There are steps that can be taken to improve the situation. For example, are there adequate incentives for farmers to grow crops in more efficient ways? Should we introduce policies that stabilize prices, so that farmers can invest in increasing crop yields? Do farmers need better roads to access markets, or credit to buy fertilizer?

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More than a billion poor people around the world are chronically malnourished and can't afford adequate food right now. If prices go higher, they will be among the first to suffer. Although it's difficult to make provision for everybody, it's also possible that the global community up to now has failed to think about the problem in the right way. Maybe we have spent too long believing that resources would eventually trickle down to the poorest groups – when increasingly the evidence suggests they're not going to. The global community has only recently begun to focus on what kind of crop investments would be needed to reach those with extremely limited resources. Institutions, such as the Gates Foundation and the Rockefeller Foundation, are trying to resolve this issue on a big scale now.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Scientists know for sure that temperatures are going to increase, which will reduce crop productivity after a certain threshold. People say, 'well, in the United States, if we have warmer temperatures, won't that increase wheat production, for example?' Yes, up to a point—then there is likely to be a huge decrease. Temperature affects evaporation and moisture stress on crops. With the temperature increases that are projected for the next 40 to 50 years, we're going to start to see a falling off in production in many parts of the world, particularly in the tropics and subtropics. As the planet warms there may be more moisture in the atmosphere overall, but it won't necessarily produce rainfall where you want it, or when you want it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Currently there is a project in Benin, West Africa, where it rains only three to four months of the year, to improve food production. Scientists working for international agencies are helping poor communities to use solar-powered drip irrigation for small plots of high-value crops. For example, the project is promoting indigenous legumes that yield more protein and fertilize the soil. People are also planting more carrots and leafy vegetables, since they are nutritious and relatively easy to cultivate. And the markets are right there in these areas. People are taking their products to market at 5 in the morning and it's all gone by 5:15. It's amazing. In villages where these techniques have been evaluated, there's been a doubling and tripling of incomes for the families involved, and nutrition has improved throughout the communities.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Although crops are probably going to be made more efficient by genetic engineering than by traditional breeding, there are a lot of crops already out there that are extremely drought and heat tolerant — we've just made the mistake of moving away from them. They've been underutilized partly because the agricultural development mentality has been to concentrate on staple foods such as wheat. It's more useful to think in terms of a diversity of crops, which involves making greater use of traditional crops. The best solutions take into account people's incomes in a particular area. The selected crops must be suitable, not just ecologically, but economically, for a specific region. The global community is beginning to recognize that food insecurity is an extremely important issue – and one that will lead to a lot of human suffering if it's not dealt with. I am, therefore, optimistic for the future and think that all sorts of innovative approaches will be brought in.

content: Crop yields around the world vary immensely. For example, while the production of certain crops in Nebraska in the USA almost reaches the production {{23}} , farmers in other parts of the world are producing approximately 50 per cent of this figure. As global temperatures increase, the problem of food production is likely to get worse. Higher temperatures may bring initial benefits such as increased levels of atmospheric {{24}} , but rainfall will be unpredictable. The most likely outcome is a large {{25}} in the amount of food produced. There are a number of possible ways in which food production can be improved. Genetically engineered crops have advantages, but there are also traditional crops that offer resistance to high temperatures and water shortages. These traditional foods were under-exploited in the past because of the tendency to produce certain common crops like {{26}} , rather than a variety of local species.

subtitle: The economist Rosamond Naylor discusses how we can meet the increasing pressures on food production.
